note: Same eight-part structure as the Korean and Japanese grammar files, and almost no overlap in content. There are no particles here in the Korean or Japanese sense, no conjugation, and no politeness levels built into the verb. What there is instead: word order, measure words, and aspect. Each point has a `simple` explanation with no terminology and a `technical` one for when the learner wants it.

points.name: 是
points.simple: 是 joins two nouns: 我是学生 — I am a student. That is all it does. If you want to say something is big, or cold, or good, 是 is the wrong word — see the next point.
points.technical: The copula, used for identity and category membership between nominals. It does not take adjectival complements; Mandarin adjectives are stative verbs and predicate directly.

examples.note: 不是 is said bú shì — 不 rises before a fourth tone.

mistakes.why: 是 links nouns. With an adjective you use 很.

points.name: 很 + adjective
points.simple:
To say something is big, you say 很大 — not 是大. The word 很 usually translates as 'very', but here it is mostly holding the sentence together, and 我很好 means 'I'm fine', not 'I'm VERY good'.

Without 很, a bare adjective sounds like a comparison: 我好 hints at 'I'm good (and someone else isn't)'.
points.technical: Mandarin adjectives are stative verbs and predicate without a copula. 很 functions as a default degree adverb whose semantic force is bleached in neutral statements; its absence triggers a contrastive reading.

examples.note: Said wó hěn hǎo — third-tone sandhi.
In the negative, 很 drops out.

points.name: 不 and 没
points.simple:
不 is about what you don't do, won't do, or never do. It is about choice and habit. 我不吃肉 means you're vegetarian.

没 is about something that did not happen. 我没吃饭 means you haven't eaten yet.

And 有 is the exception that never bends: it is always 没有, never 不有.
points.technical: 不 negates volition, habitual action and stative predicates; 没(有) negates the realisation of an event and is incompatible with 了. 有 is lexically restricted to 没 negation.

examples.note: Future intention takes 不, not 没.

mistakes.why: 有 is only ever negated with 没.
Liking is a state, not an event that failed to happen.

points.name: 吗 questions
points.meaning: turning a statement into a yes/no question
points.simple:
Say the statement, then add 吗 at the end. Nothing else moves. 你是学生 is 'you are a student'; 你是学生吗？is 'are you a student?'

This is far easier than English, which has to shuffle the words around.
points.technical: A sentence-final interrogative particle forming polar questions with no change to constituent order. Always neutral tone.

points.name: Question words stay put
points.structure: the question word sits where the answer would sit
points.simple:
In English, 'what' jumps to the front: 'What are you eating?' In Mandarin it stays exactly where the answer goes.

你吃什么？— literally 'you eat what?'
他是谁？— 'he is who?'
你去哪儿？— 'you go where?'

So to ask a question, take the answer and swap in the question word. Nothing moves, and you do not add 吗.
points.technical: Mandarin is wh-in-situ. Interrogative pronouns remain in argument position; no fronting and no auxiliary inversion. 吗 is incompatible with a wh-word in the same clause.

mistakes.why: The question word does not move to the front.

points.name: 的
points.simple:
的 attaches a description to a noun. 我的书 is 'my book'. 老师的车 is 'the teacher's car'. The order is the reverse of English's 'of': the owner comes first.

It is dropped for close relationships and for the place you belong to: 我妈妈, not 我的妈妈. 我们学校, not 我们的学校.
points.technical: A subordinating particle marking a modifier–head relation. Omitted with inalienable possession, kinship terms and institutional membership when the modifier is a pronoun.

examples.note: 的 also attaches a whole descriptive phrase.

points.name: Measure words
points.simple:
You cannot say 'three books' in Mandarin. You say 'three [bound-thing] book' — 三本书.

English does this too, but only for some words: 'two slices of bread', 'three sheets of paper'. Mandarin does it for everything.

本 for books. 张 for flat things. 只 for animals. 条 for long floppy things. 杯 for cups of something. And 个 for everything else, which is what to use when you cannot remember.
points.technical: Mandarin nouns are non-count and require a classifier between a determiner or numeral and the noun. Classifier choice is lexically determined and only loosely predictable from the noun's semantics.

examples.note: 两, not 二, before a measure word.
这 and 那 need one too.

mistakes.why: A number can never sit directly against a noun.
Before a measure word, two is 两.

points.name: 有
points.structure: Subject + 有 + object   /   Place + 有 + thing
points.simple:
有 does two jobs. With a person in front it means 'have': 我有一本书.

With a place in front it means 'there is': 桌子上有一本书 — 'on the table there is a book'.

Its negative is 没有, always.
points.technical: An existential and possessive verb. In the existential frame the locative phrase is the subject and the possessed noun is typically indefinite.

examples.pinyin: zhuōzi shàng yǒu yì běn shū
examples.english: There's a book on the table.

examples.note: 有没有 is a very common way to ask a yes/no question.

points.name: 了
points.simple:
了 is NOT the past tense. Mandarin has no past tense.

了 says one of two things. After a verb, it says the action finished: 我吃了饭 — I've eaten.

At the end of a sentence, it says something has changed: 下雨了 — it's started raining. That one is about right now, not the past.

And 明天我就走了 has 了 and is about tomorrow. If you want to say when something happened, use a time word — 昨天, 明天. That is where time lives in this language.
points.technical: An aspect marker with two positions. Verb-final 了 (perfective -le) marks a bounded event; sentence-final 了 (inchoative le) marks a change of state or newly relevant situation. Neither encodes tense; temporal reference is adverbial.

examples.note: Past — and no 了, because it describes a habit rather than an event.

mistakes.why: One 了 is enough; piling them up does not make it more past.

points.name: Word order
points.structure: Subject — Time — Place — Manner — Verb — Object
points.simple:
Everything that sets the scene comes BEFORE the verb.

English: 'I'm going to Beijing tomorrow.' Time at the end.
Mandarin: 我明天去北京 — literally 'I tomorrow go Beijing'. Time before the verb.

Same for place: 我在图书馆看书 — 'I at library read books'.

And where two time words meet, the bigger one comes first: 明天早上, not 早上明天.
points.technical: SVO with strictly pre-verbal adjuncts. Temporal and locative phrases are ordered from larger to smaller scope and precede the verb phrase; post-verbal position is reserved for objects and complements.

mistakes.why: Time never goes at the end.

points.name: 在
points.meaning: being somewhere, and doing something now
points.structure: Subject + 在 + place   /   Subject + 在 + verb
points.simple:
在 before a place means 'at': 我在家 — I'm at home.

在 before a verb means the action is happening right now: 我在吃饭 — I'm eating.

Same word, two jobs, and which one it is depends on what comes after it.
points.technical: A locative verb and preposition; pre-verbally it functions as a progressive aspect marker. Distinct from 着, which marks a resultant state rather than an ongoing action.

examples.note: Both jobs at once: 在学校 is the place, and it sits before the verb.
着, not 在 — a state, not an action.

points.name: 会, 能, 想
points.simple:
会 — you learned how. 我会说汉语 — I can speak Chinese, because I studied it.

能 — you are able to right now. 我今天不能来 — I can't come today, because something is in the way.

想 — you want to. 我想喝茶 — I'd like some tea.

All three sit in front of the verb, and none of them change shape.
points.technical: Pre-verbal modal auxiliaries. 会 encodes acquired ability and, separately, future likelihood; 能 encodes circumstantial possibility and permission; 想 encodes desire or intention. Negation is with 不 in all three cases.

mistakes.why: A learned skill takes 会. 能 would suggest something is temporarily allowing you to speak.
